II. DESCRIPTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
Introduction. The environment that will be affected by the proposed legislation will be the entire physical and part of the economic. The physical environment, in this sense, consists of the collective habitats of the endangered animals and of the humans that live in association with them. This environment can be as great in extent as the entire surface of the earth—but will likely be somewhat less, as we will demonstrate in the following pages. It will be both continental and marine, terrestrial and aquatic, equatorial and polar. Every habitat which supports some form of life is an environment that may be impacted.
The economic environment, on the other hand, is the trade generated by animals and animal products both on a national and worldwide scale. Such trade involves not only the sale of live animals and their parts, but products that unificative from these parts and which ultimately reach a consumer. Another aspect of this economic environment is the land development and alteration of habitat that will be curtailed because of the needs of endangered species.

Also part of the economic environment is the loss of livestock and farm crops that may occur because of depredating and foraging endangered animals.
Members of the animal groups potentially subject to the provisions of the proposed legislation may be found at one time or another in virtually every "corner" of the earth. To be eligible for benefits under the Act, however, the species or subspecies must be regarded by the Secretary as endangered as defined by the proposed legislation. To a large extent, determination of which species and subspecies should be regarded as endangered is limited by a lack of knowledge.
